analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue federal agents for money damages when federal officials violate their constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill would have let people sue federal officials for money damages over constitutional rights violations, but with 11 Democratic cosponsors and no hearing, it died in committee when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Bivens Act would amend the federal civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) so it covers violations by people acting under federal authority, not just state and local officials [S2]. Today, someone whose rights are violated by a federal agent — a Border Patrol officer, an ICE agent, an FBI agent — has almost no practical way to win money damages, because the Supreme Court has repeatedly narrowed the judge-made exception (called "Bivens") that once allowed such suits. This bill would write the remedy into law directly, letting the victim sue the officer in federal court [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose constitutional rights are violated by federal officials — for example, people subjected to unlawful searches, excessive force, or detention by Border Patrol, ICE, FBI, or other federal agents. They would gain a clear statutory right to sue the officer for money damages in federal court, instead of the near-total lack of remedy that exists today after the Supreme Court limited the old Bivens case law. People hurt by federal overreach at the border and in immigration enforcement would be among the clearest winners, since that is where federal agents most often act without a state-level remedy.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends Section 1983 of the Revised Statutes (42 U.S.C. 1983), the main civil rights law people use to sue officials, by adding 'of the United States' alongside state and local governments — making federal officials subject to the same civil damages remedy as state and local ones.

It gives a person whose rights were violated by 'a person acting under Federal authority' a civil cause of action, which is exactly the remedy gap left open after the Supreme Court sharply limited the judge-made Bivens exception for suing federal officers (Ziglar v. Abbasi, Egbert v. Boule).

Because it writes the remedy into statute rather than leaving it to courts, victims would no longer depend on the Supreme Court's willingness to recognize new Bivens claims, which it has refused to do in recent years.

analysis.who_pays: Federal officials who violate rights would face personal liability for damages, and federal agencies (and ultimately taxpayers) would bear the costs of judgments, settlements, and legal defense, since agencies routinely indemnify officers. Federal law enforcement agencies would also face more litigation overall.

drawbacks.text: The bill exposes federal officers to personal lawsuits, and as written it is a single-line insertion into Section 1983 that does not spell out how defenses like qualified immunity would apply to federal officers — leaving the practical scope of liability to be worked out in litigation.

The costs of judgments and settlements against federal officers would largely be passed through agency indemnification to taxpayers, and the added litigation exposure would raise defense costs for federal agencies.

Police and law enforcement organizations argue that broad personal liability deters people from taking jobs in federal law enforcement and makes officers hesitant to act in fast-moving situations; an honest supporter would acknowledge this tension and could address it with clearer statutory protections for good-faith conduct.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: it closes a genuine accountability gap, giving people harmed by federal agents the same basic right to sue that they already have against state and local police. The cost is increased litigation against federal officers and, through indemnification, against the treasury, plus uncertainty about how officer defenses would be handled. The remedy could have been paired with explicit statutory protection for officers acting in good faith to limit that downside; the bill as introduced did not do that. On balance, the accountability gain outweighs the litigation cost, but the design was thin.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final months of the session and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote, and it expired when Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson introduced the Bivens Act on August 2, 2024, with 11 cosponsors, all Democrats, including Jamie Raskin, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, and Pramila Jayapal.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary — and that is the last action ever taken on it.

The committee, controlled by Republicans, never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, meaning it would have to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies and officers are better off, because they face no new civil liability for violating constitutional rights. People harmed by federal agents remain without a practical damages remedy.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal agencies and officers facing no new liability

for.name: Rep. Hank C. 'Hank' Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Bivens Act and recruited 11 cosponsors for it.

for.name: Jamie Raskin and 10 other House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill its entire bloc of support.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership (Chair Jim Jordan)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote after its referral, letting it die in committee.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority controlling the House agenda and committee calendar
against.what_they_did: Brought no Republican cosponsors and allowed no floor action on a bill expanding liability for federal officers.

against.name: Law enforcement organizations
against.role: Police unions and federal officer associations
against.what_they_did: Long opposed expanding civil liability for officers, the same posture that shapes Republican resistance to such bills.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters — the sponsor and 11 cosponsors — were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies and officers (Border Patrol, ICE, FBI, etc.)
industries.note: The bill would expose federal officers to the same civil damages suits state and local police already face, ending the effective shield created by the Supreme Court's narrowing of Bivens. Agencies and officers resisted through the Republican majority, and the bill never got a hearing.

A statutory cause of action against federal officials would open a large new field of civil rights litigation, with fees typically recoverable from defendants under related provisions. The bill's death keeps that market closed.

Judgments and settlements against officers are generally paid by the government, so the remedy's cost would land on the treasury in exchange for a real deterrent against misconduct. No liability was created because the bill died.
